meta.title: Who really said "I Have Never Killed Any One, But I Have Read Some Obituary Notices with Great Satisfaction"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain. The line is Clarence Darrow's, from his 1932 memoir The Story of My Life — sharpened from a speech he gave in 1922.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Have Never Killed Any One, But I Have Read Some Obituary Notices with Great Satisfaction'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mark Twain. It's Clarence Darrow, word for word, in his 1932 autobiography — and he was arguing against the death penalty.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — actually Clarence Darrow
answer.authorDates: 1857–1938 · American defense lawyer and civil libertarian
answer.sourceLine: This is Darrow’s wording, word for word, from his 1932 autobiography The Story of My Life. He had been sharpening the same joke for a decade — a looser version in a 1922 speech, another in 1926 congressional testimony against the death penalty — before it settled into the one-liner people now pin on Twain, who died in 1910.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Ch. 10, “Child Training” — page 86 in the Da Capo Press reprint cited by Quote Investigator
Speech, “Crime,” Illinois Conference on Public Welfare, 13 November 1922

source.excerpt: All men have an emotion to kill; when they strongly dislike some one they involuntarily wish he was dead. I have never killed any one, but I have read some obituary notices with great satisfaction.
trail: 13 November 1922 — addressing the Illinois Conference on Public Welfare in a speech titled “Crime,” Darrow says he never killed anybody but has had “a great deal of satisfaction over many obituary notices” that he has read. This is the earliest instance Quote Investigator located ↗.

February 1926 — testifying to a US House committee on abolishing capital punishment in the District of Columbia, Darrow argues “we are all murderers at heart” and repeats the line. The New York Times report of 2 February 1926 renders it as “I have often read obituary notices with considerable satisfaction,” a wording that differs from the government transcript — both are quoted and cited by QI ↗.
1932 — the polished form appears in The Story of My Life, ch. 10, where Wikiquote records it in its sourced section ↗ with the surrounding paragraph intact.
2011 onward — a loosened version begins circulating online credited to Mark Twain; Snopes rates that credit “Incorrect Attribution” ↗ and points back to Darrow’s 1932 sentence.
source.excerptNote: The famous sentence is the second half of the passage. Wikiquote’s sourced entry prints a longer run of the paragraph, which begins “Every instinct that is found in any man is in all men” — the argument the joke is serving.

Darrow’s earlier and differently worded 1922 and 1926 versions appear in state and federal publications that are themselves free of restriction, but those are not this wording.

author.name: Clarence Darrow
author.heading: Who was Clarence Darrow?
author.metaLine: 1857–1938 · American defense lawyer, agnostic, and opponent of capital punishment
author.bio: Clarence Darrow was the most famous defense attorney in America, remembered for the Leopold and Loeb case, the 1925 Scopes “Monkey” Trial, and his defense of Ossian Sweet. He built a career on the argument that no one is purely innocent — that the impulses society punishes are present in everybody — which is exactly the argument the obituary line was written to serve. He published The Story of My Life in 1932, six years before his death.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: Twain is the default owner of any unclaimed American wisecrack, and this one has been his online since about 2011 — usually in a reworded form that Darrow never wrote either.

items.why: Twain died on 21 April 1910, twelve years before Darrow’s earliest known use of the joke. Wikiquote files a reworded version in Twain’s Misattributed section ↗ and identifies it as a misquotation of Darrow.

items.who: “I’ve never wished a man dead, but I have read some obituaries with great pleasure”
items.why: This is the form that circulates on social media under Twain’s name. Snopes rates it “Incorrect Attribution” ↗ and traces it to Darrow’s 1932 sentence — it is neither Twain’s nor Darrow’s actual wording.
Churchill is the other standing magnet for orphaned epigrams; Wikiquote’s Darrow entry notes ↗ that the misquoted version has been credited to him among others.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence, exactly as written above, is Clarence Darrow’s — published in The Story of My Life in 1932 and traced back to a 1922 speech by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Darrow was not making a dinner-party joke. He was making an argument about the death penalty, and the line was the hinge of it. Testifying before a House committee in February 1926 on abolishing capital punishment in the District of Columbia, he told the room that everyone is a murderer at heart — that he had never taken a life himself, but had read obituary notices with satisfaction, and so had they. If the impulse is universal, he was saying, the state has no clean standing to kill for it.

The 1932 memoir version keeps the same logic and cuts the words. It arrives after the sentence “All men have an emotion to kill; when they strongly dislike some one they involuntarily wish he was dead” — the setup that makes the punchline an indictment rather than a wisecrack. Stripped of that setup and repotted under Twain’s name, it reads as harmless mischief, which is roughly the opposite of what Darrow meant.
detailsBody: 1922 — the long form: he never killed anybody, but has “had a great deal of satisfaction over many obituary notices.” Funny, but slack.
1926 — tighter, and pointed at Congress: “I never killed anybody, but I often read an obituary notice with great satisfaction.”
1932 — the finished epigram, and the wording that travels today.

2007 onward — anthologies begin printing a “pleasure” variant, still credited to Darrow. By 2011 the same shape is circulating online under Twain’s name, usually as “I’ve never wished a man dead, but I have read some obituaries with great pleasure.”
context.pull: Darrow’s joke was an argument against executions. Twain’s version is just a joke.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Clarence Darrow originated the quip, documents a 13 November 1922 speech 'Crime' to the Illinois Conference on Public Welfare as the earliest instance it located, a February 1926 US House committee appearance on capital punishment, the New York Times report of 2 February 1926 ('I have often read obituary notices with considerable satisfaction'), and the 1932 memoir wording 'I have never killed any one, but I have read some obituary notices with great satisfaction' (cited to page 86 of the Da Capo reprint), plus an 1908 Overland Monthly precursor and a 2007 'pleasure' variant.

Wikiquote's Clarence Darrow page carries the exact sentence in its sourced section under 'The Story of My Life (1932)', ch. 10 'Child Training', preceded by 'All men have an emotion to kill; when they strongly dislike some one they involuntarily wish he was dead', and notes the line has been misquoted and attributed to Mark Twain and Winston Churchill among others.
Wikiquote's Mark Twain page lists 'I have never killed a man, but I have read many obituaries with great pleasure' in its Misattributed section, describing it as a misquotation of Clarence Darrow.

Snopes rates the claim that Mark Twain said 'I've never wished a man dead, but I have read some obituaries with great pleasure' as 'Incorrect Attribution', and states it likely originated as a misquotation of Clarence Darrow's 1932 line 'I have never killed any one, but I have read some obituary notices with great satisfaction', circulating in that form under Twain's name from 2011.

Clarence Darrow lived 18 April 1857 to 13 March 1938, was an American lawyer known for Leopold and Loeb, the Scopes trial and the Ossian Sweet defense, and published The Story of My Life with Charles Scribner's Sons in 1932.
Mark Twain (Samuel Langhorne Clemens) was born 30 November 1835 and died 21 April 1910 — before any of Darrow's documented uses of the line.
The Internet Archive holds a scanned 1932 printing of Clarence Darrow's The Story of My Life (Grosset and Dunlap), available through its lending library.

TruthOrFiction's write-up attributes the quote to Clarence Darrow rather than Mark Twain, citing the 1922 speech, 1926 congressional testimony and the 1932 autobiography, and notes The Atlantic's 3 May 2011 statement that Twain never said it.
